title: A Third of Americans May Have Fatty Liver Disease — Diet Is the Fix
excerpt: Up to 42% of American adults may have fat building up in their livers without knowing it. Doctors say the fix isn't a cleanse — it's what you eat every day.
body:
• Between 30% and 40% of American adults have excess fat stored in their livers, a condition called MASLD — and most have no symptoms, according to the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases.
  • Gastroenterologists say there is no detox, cleanse, or supplement that clears liver fat; a Mediterranean-style diet, cutting added sugar and refined carbs, and sustained weight loss are the first-line treatments.
  • Research links highly processed foods, sugary drinks, fast food, and commercially prepared fructose to liver inflammation and scarring.
  • Eating more fiber, whole foods, fish, nuts, and olive oil — and keeping alcohol and sugary drinks in check — protects the liver over time.

A startling share of Americans are walking around with a fatty liver and have no idea. Between 30% and 40% of adults in the United States have metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), the condition formerly known as nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, according to the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases. Some estimates put the figure as high as 42%. The organ silently stores excess fat until, in a significant minority of cases, it progresses to inflammation, scarring, cirrhosis, or even liver cancer.

The condition has become one of the most common causes of liver disease in the country, alongside a sharp rise in obesity and type 2 diabetes. Patients with fatty liver disease also face a heightened risk of cardiovascular disease. With cases climbing, gastroenterologists are using the moment to say plainly what the science supports — and what it does not.

What doctors say actually works

The American Gastroenterological Association's clinical practice guidance, published in the journal Gastroenterology, calls lifestyle modification the cornerstone of treatment: a hypocaloric Mediterranean-style diet — fresh vegetables, fruit, legumes, minimally processed whole grains, fish, olive oil, nuts, and seeds — paired with exercise and weight loss. "Weight loss is associated with a reduction in liver fat, which provides a potential for reversal of disease progression," wrote Zobair M. Younossi of Inova Fairfax Medical Campus, the lead author of the AGA update. Clinically meaningful weight loss typically requires eating 1,200 to 1,500 calories a day, or cutting 500 to 1,000 calories from baseline intake.

Hepatologists echo the advice. In an interview with Parade, Dr. Jasmohan Bajaj, a professor at Virginia Commonwealth University's Stravitz-Sanyal Institute for Liver Disease and Metabolic Health, pointed to high-fiber foods as especially protective. Research shows that fiber-rich diets lower the risk of MASLD.

"Highly processed diets rich in saturated fats, trans fats and ultra-processed foods may promote inflammation, which can worsen liver disease and contribute to scarring. Poor dietary patterns can increase insulin resistance, causing the liver to produce and store more fat."

— Dr. Kais, hepatologist, in an interview with Parade

The foods to cut

The list of liver-unfriendly foods will surprise no one, but doctors say the scale of intake matters more than people realize. Sugary drinks, candy, desserts, white bread and highly processed grains, frequent fast food, and excess calories from any source all drive fat accumulation in the liver. Fructose from whole fruit is not associated with fatty liver, but commercially prepared fructose — the kind sweetening sodas and packaged snacks — has been linked to visceral fat, insulin resistance, liver inflammation, and fibrosis progression.

What won't help, doctors stress, is the booming market of liver "cleanses" and detox teas. A gastroenterologist who spoke to the Hindustan Times put it bluntly: there is no magic liver detox or cleanse. No supplement has been shown to clear fat from the liver; only sustained dietary change and weight loss do that.

Why it matters for the diaspora

The warning carries particular weight for Indian-American households, where restaurant portions, rich festive foods, and long sedentary workdays combine into exactly the dietary pattern hepatologists flag. Because South Asian adults tend to develop insulin resistance and metabolic disease at lower body weights, the same waistline that looks unremarkable can hide a stressed liver — making regular checkups and dietary discipline matters of family health, not just personal choice.

What to watch

Doctors say the first step is a conversation, not a cleanse. Harvard Health notes that screening for fatty liver disease typically starts with blood work and imaging for people with obesity, diabetes, or abnormal liver enzymes — and caught early, the condition is one of the few liver diseases that can be reversed. With no shortcut in sight, the guidance remains unglamorous and effective: eat like the Mediterranean diet, drink water instead of soda, and give the liver less to store and more time to heal.
